newsitem.title: UK: Plan to convert ENI zinc smelter hits snag.
newsitem.headline: Plan to convert ENI zinc smelter hits snag.

text.p: Osmium Holdings, a group of British and U.S. investors, has run into problems in its plans to buy Italy's Crotone zinc smelter and convert it into a nickel-copper refinery, a company spokesman said.
Russia's Norilsk Nickel has insisted on reviewing an agreement to supply concentrates, said Keith Irons, chairman of Bankside Consultants, which is representing Osmium.

As a result, Osmium this week was forced to tell Ente Nazionale Idrocarburi Spa (ENI) -- the giant Italian state owned energy group that owns the smelter -- that it would not be able to meet a end-July deadline to buy the facility.
"It is a great disappointment...but Osmium are still greatly committed to the whole project," he added in a telephone interview.
"If the deal can get back on track before the end of this year, then there's a possibility to renegotiate an arrangement with ENI," Irons said.
Osmium had a memorandum of understanding with ENI to buy the smelter, which included an end-July deadline.
Under the plan the 100,000-tonne per year Italian facility, owned by ENI-unit Pertusola Sud SpA, was to have been closed for conversion sometime next year.
The metals market has been closely following the progress of the deal, since the closure would remove supply of zinc, a star performer this year on the London Metal Exchange (LME).
Three-month zinc prices this week surged to a 6-3/4 year high of $1,507 per tonne on the LME, up from $1,057 at the beginning of the year.

Osmium last year signed agreements with Norilsk to process 11 million tonnes of low-grade concentrate in Russia, from tailings dams which collect residues, then ship the higher-grade concentrate to Italy for refining.

But a change in management at Norilsk led to a series of renegotiations, which culminated in Norilsk recently saying they were not in a position to proceed because they wished to determine whether they could process the tailings themselves.
The review by Norilsk is expected to take two to three months.
"Hopefully there will be further discussions with Norilsk in due time, but nothing is going to happen until they complete their review," Irons said.
"Osmium does have legally binding agreements to take the tailings from two dams," he added.
But Osmium was not currently considering taking legal action against Norilsk. "I think that is an issue that is yet not being considered," Irons said.
Osmium's investors include Mark Jones III, chairman of Crown Resources Corp. SBC Warburgs are the financial advisers for the project, Irons said.
